chapter_summary:
Having mastered the basics of attributes and VEX, it's time to explore more sophisticated techniques for manipulating and transferring data. Often, you'll find yourself needing to move attribute data from one part of your geometry to another, or even from one piece of geometry to an entirely different one. Houdini provides several powerful SOPs and VEX functions specifically designed for these tasks, which are indispensable for building complex procedural assets and effects, especially in game development where data consistency across different LODs or meshes is critical.

The **Attribute Transfer SOP** is a workhorse for projecting attributes from a source geometry onto a destination geometry based on proximity. Imagine you have a high-detail sculpt with vertex colors representing wear and tear, and you want to transfer these colors onto a low-poly game mesh. The `Attribute Transfer` node takes two inputs: the source (with the attributes) and the destination (where attributes will be transferred). You specify which attributes to transfer (e.g., `Cd`, `N`, `uv`) and control the transfer using parameters like `Distance Threshold` and `Blend Width`. Points on the destination geometry will look for nearby points on the source geometry and interpolate their attribute values. This is incredibly useful for baking details, projecting textures, or transferring custom data like vertex weights or masks from one mesh to another. A common pitfall is setting the `Distance Threshold` too low, resulting in patchy transfers, or too high, leading to unwanted bleeding of attributes. Always visualize the transfer and adjust the threshold carefully.

Next, the **Attribute Promote SOP** is essential when you need to change the *class* of an attribute. For example, you might have a `Cd` attribute on your points, but for a specific operation, you need it to be a primitive attribute (e.g., to assign a material per face). `Attribute Promote` allows you to convert point attributes to primitive, primitive to point, or even detail attributes to other classes. When promoting from a finer granularity (like point) to a coarser one (like primitive), you need to specify a `Promotion Method` (e.g., `Average`, `Sum`, `Min`, `Max`). If you promote `Cd` from points to primitives using `Average`, each primitive's color will become the average of the colors of its constituent points. Conversely, promoting from primitive to point will typically assign the primitive's attribute value to all its points. This node is vital for adapting attribute data to different stages of your procedural pipeline.

The **Attribute Copy SOP** is used when you need to copy attributes from one geometry to another *without* relying on proximity. Instead, it typically copies attributes based on matching point or primitive numbers, or by using a custom attribute as an ID. This is particularly useful when you have two geometries that are topologically identical or have a consistent ordering, and you just want to duplicate specific attributes. For instance, if you've run a simulation on a proxy mesh and want to copy the velocity (`v`) attribute back to your original high-res mesh that has the same point count and order, `Attribute Copy` is the perfect tool. It's faster and more precise than `Attribute Transfer` when topology matches.

Beyond these SOPs, VEX offers powerful functions for **cross-component data access**. We briefly mentioned `prim()` and `point()` in the previous chapter. These allow you to read attributes from a different component type than the one your wrangle is currently running over. For example, if you're iterating over points, `prim(0, "Cd", @primnum)` lets you read the color of the primitive that the current point belongs to. This is crucial for creating complex relationships between different parts of your geometry. Similarly, `point(0, "P", @ptnum)` can read the position of a specific point when you're in a primitive wrangle.

Finally, understanding **attribute interpolation** is key to effective data transfer. When attributes are transferred or promoted, values are often interpolated between existing data points. For `Attribute Transfer`, the `Blend Width` parameter controls how smoothly attributes are interpolated across the distance threshold. For `Attribute Promote` from point to primitive, the `Average` method is a form of interpolation. This ensures smooth transitions and prevents harsh, pixelated results. In game development, accurate attribute interpolation is critical for things like vertex lighting, blending textures, or smooth animation weights. Always consider how your attribute values will behave when they are averaged, blended, or projected, and adjust your parameters to achieve the desired visual or functional outcome.

screens.title: Advanced Attribute Manipulation and Transfer
screens.subtitle: Project, promote, and copy attribute data between geometry with precision

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn practical methods to move attribute data reliably between shapes. We'll focus on three SOPs that solve most attribute problems: Attribute Transfer for proximity-based projection, Attribute Promote for changing an attribute's class, and Attribute Copy for index- or ID-based duplication. You will also see how VEX functions like prim() and point() let you read values across component types, and why interpolation choices such as blend width or averaging matter for smooth results. A concrete scenario ties these ideas together: project vertex color from a detailed sphere onto a low-polygon box, then promote that color to a single detail value for downstream logic. Along the way I will point out common pitfalls—thresholds that are too small, topology mismatches, and unintended averaging—and show how to validate your results in the geometry spreadsheet. By the end you will understand which tool fits each situation and how to tune parameters so your transfers are clean and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Reliable attribute transfer and class changes let you bake detail, preserve animation data, and prepare assets for game or render pipelines. Parameter tuning and the right SOP choice make the difference between noisy results and professional, production-ready meshes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: In these two objective screens we break the chapter into concrete, testable skills. First, you'll gain practical command of the Attribute Transfer SOP: how it finds nearby points, which attributes it can move, and how Distance Threshold plus Blend Width shape the result. You'll practice transferring color and weight data from a dense mesh to a low-poly target, learning to spot patchiness versus unwanted bleeding. Second, you'll learn the Attribute Promote SOP: how and why to change an attribute's class. You will compare promotion methods such as Average, Sum, Min, and Max and see how promoting from point to primitive changes the data granularity. Third, you will use Attribute Copy when topologies match, learning the benefits of index-based copying versus proximity projection. Finally, you will read and write cross-component data with VEX using prim() and point(), and understand attribute interpolation mechanics so your transfers are smooth. Each skill includes a verification milestone so you can confirm competency in the geometry spreadsheet.

keyIdea.title: Practical outcomes

screens.title: Attribute Transfer SOP — What and Why
screens.subtitle: Project attributes from a source to a destination using proximity

narration.text: Attribute Transfer projects attribute values from one geometry onto another using spatial proximity. The node requires a source and a destination input; destination points search for nearby source points and interpolate attribute values such as Cd, N, uv, or custom masks. This is ideal when you have a detailed mesh—like a sculpt with painted vertex color—and you want to bake that look onto a low-resolution game mesh. A concrete example is transferring a colorful ramp stored on a dense sphere to a box with few divisions: destination points within the Distance Threshold sample nearby source points and receive blended colors according to the Blend Width. A common misconception is thinking larger thresholds always improve results; in fact, an overly large Distance Threshold can cause attributes to bleed from distant features and lose localized detail. Another mistake is attempting Attribute Transfer when the meshes have identical topology—Attribute Copy is both faster and more precise for that case. As a closing check, always inspect the geometry spreadsheet to confirm transferred attribute presence and use visualizers to catch patchy coverage. How might you choose Distance Threshold and Blend Width for a very thin target mesh?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Attribute Transfer projects attributes by proximity and interpolates values using distance and blend controls; tune thresholds to balance coverage and locality.

content.html:
Core Concept

Attribute Transfer SOP

Project attributes by proximity from source to destination. Control which attributes to transfer and how values are blended across distance.

Key parameters
  • Attributes to Transfer — list which attribute names are copied (e.g., Cd, N, uv).
  • Distance Threshold — maximum search radius for source points.
  • Blend Width — falloff for interpolation inside the threshold.
Example
Project Cd from a high-res sphere onto a low-res box, then visualize with a Color SOP set to From Attributes.
Key Takeaway

Use Attribute Transfer when geometries differ topologically but have similar shapes; tune distance and blend to control locality and smoothness.

Transfer Workflow (visualized as cards)
Source
High-res mesh with Cd ramp applied via Attribute Wrangle.
Transfer
Attribute Transfer: set Cd in Attributes to Transfer, adjust threshold and blend.
Destination
Low-poly box receives attribute and visualizes with Color From Attributes.
Troubleshooting tips
  • Too patchy: increase Distance Threshold slightly or add more source density.
  • Unwanted bleeding: reduce Distance Threshold or tighten Blend Width.
  • Topology matches? Consider Attribute Copy instead for exactness.

screens.title: Tuning Transfer Parameters
screens.subtitle: Distance Threshold, Blend Width, and attribute selection

narration.text: Tuning parameters is the practical heart of successful attribute transfer. Start by selecting the attributes you need to transfer and keep the list minimal—extra attributes increase computation and risk unintended side effects. For Distance Threshold, choose a value large enough so destination points find meaningful source neighbors, but not so large that distant features bleed into unrelated areas. For a thin target mesh, a slightly smaller threshold with a carefully increased source density often beats a single large threshold. Blend Width controls how softly attribute values fall off inside the threshold. A small blend yields sharp transitions that preserve edges, while a larger blend smooths values over space. A quick workflow: set Attributes to Transfer, set Distance Threshold to an estimated value that covers the closest source surface, then gradually increase Blend Width to produce the desired smoothness. Verify results by viewing the geometry spreadsheet and by switching to the Color SOP set to From Attributes. A common misconception is to tune only one parameter; in practice you must balance threshold and blend together. Try a few render or viewport checks and ask: does the transfer preserve the local detail I care about?

keyIdea.title: Tuning rule
keyIdea.text: Balance Distance Threshold and Blend Width together; visualize and use the spreadsheet to confirm coverage and smoothing.

content.html:
Process Flow

Tune Transfer Parameters

1. Select Attributes
Choose only necessary names like Cd, v, uv to avoid copying excess data.
2. Estimate Distance Threshold
Start with a radius that reaches the nearby source surface; increase if coverage is sparse.
3. Adjust Blend Width
Raise for smooth blending, lower for sharper attribute edges.
4. Validate
Use Color From Attributes and geometry spreadsheet to confirm values and distribution.
Concrete Scenario
You have a sphere with a vertical Cd ramp and a low-poly box. Set Distance Threshold to about the average distance from box points to the sphere surface. If you see isolated points without color, slightly increase the threshold. If colors spread across faces that should be different, reduce the threshold or tighten the blend.
Common Mistake
Treating Blend Width as unrelated to Distance Threshold. Blend only affects falloff inside the threshold; both parameters must be tuned together.
Key Takeaway

Tune threshold for coverage and blend for smoothness, then verify visually and in the spreadsheet.

screens.title: Attribute Promote SOP — Change an attribute's class
screens.subtitle: Promote attributes between point, primitive, and detail classes

narration.text: Attribute Promote changes the class or granularity of an attribute. You might start with Cd on points but need a per-face color for material assignment, or you might want a single detail attribute that summarizes many values. Promoting from a finer class to a coarser one—point to primitive or detail—requires choosing a promotion method such as Average, Sum, Min, or Max. For example, promoting Cd from points to primitives with Average computes each primitive's color as the mean of its corner points, which yields smooth, representative face colors. Promoting from primitive to point typically assigns the primitive's value to each of its points, which can be useful when a face-driven property must be visible on vertices. A misconception is that Promote only changes names; in fact it can fundamentally change data meaning because aggregation changes magnitude and distribution. Always inspect the geometry spreadsheet after promotion. When you need a custom aggregation, consider writing a short VEX wrangle to compute a tailored detail attribute instead of relying on default methods. Attribute Promote SOP — Change an attribute's class means attribute promote converts attribute classes and aggregates values; choose the promotion method to control how fine-grain data condenses into coarser representations.. In practical terms, promote attributes between point, primitive, and detail classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Attribute Promote converts attribute classes and aggregates values; choose the promotion method to control how fine-grain data condenses into coarser representations.

content.html:
Definition

Attribute Promote

Change an attribute's class between point, primitive, and detail. Choose a method to aggregate when going from finer to coarser granularity.

Average
Compute mean value for coarser class.
Sum / Min / Max
Use when totals or extrema are required.
Example
Promote point Cd to Detail with Average to produce a single representative color you can use for whole-geometry logic or exported metadata.
Impact and gotchas
  • Promoting to a coarser class aggregates values; understand the method's effect on numeric magnitudes.
  • Promoting to a finer class usually duplicates values across new elements, which may be acceptable or require smoothing later.
  • When promoting color attributes, perceptual averaging may not always produce the visual result you expect; validate in the viewport.
Key Takeaway

Choose promotion methods deliberately: Average for smooth representative values, Sum for totals, Min/Max for bounds. Inspect results in the spreadsheet.

screens.title: Attribute Promote — Examples and Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: How promotion methods change results in practice

narration.text: Let's compare common promotion directions and what to expect. When promoting point Cd to primitive with Average, each face gets the mean of its corner vertex colors. This usually yields a visually plausible per-face color and is safe for material assignment. If you promote primitive Cd to points, Houdini typically assigns the primitive value to all associated points, which can create hard seams where faces meet. A common pitfall is promoting a weight map by Average and assuming the sum remains the same; Average reduces magnitudes when multiple points contribute. Another issue arises when promoting to Detail for global statistics: Detail Average yields a single number but loses spatial variance—useful for metadata, but not for rendering. For precise control, write a short wrangle to compute custom aggregates or to normalize after promotion. As an example, to compute average velocity as a detail attribute you can either use Attribute Promote with Average or sum all point velocities in a detail wrangle using npoints() and point() to compute an explicit mean. Which approach you pick depends on whether you need simple aggregation or a custom normalization step.

keyIdea.title: Promotion contrast
keyIdea.text: Promotion direction and method affect magnitude and distribution; verify numeric meaning after aggregation and consider custom VEX for precise control.

content.html:
Comparison

Promotion Examples

Point → Primitive (Average)
Each primitive's value becomes the average of its points. Good for per-face material colors.
Primitive → Point
Primitive values are assigned to constituent points, which can create sharp seams between faces.
Point → Detail (Average)
Computes a single representative value for the whole geometry. Useful for global metadata or thresholds.
Pitfalls & Fixes
  • Assuming sums are preserved by Average. If totals matter, use Sum or compute manually with VEX.
  • Visual seams when promoting primitive values to points; consider smoothing after promotion if needed.
  • Detail attributes discard spatial detail; use them only for metadata or single-value controls.
Check Your Understanding

If you need the total weight preserved across promotion, which method should you choose and why?

screens.title: Attribute Copy SOP — Exact Matches
screens.subtitle: Copy attributes between geometries by index or ID

narration.text: Attribute Copy duplicates attributes from one geometry to another based on matching indices or a shared ID, rather than spatial proximity. This makes it perfect when you have a high-res mesh and a low-res proxy that nevertheless share point ordering or an explicit ID attribute. A typical use case is running a fast simulation on a proxy, then copying back results such as velocity to the original mesh that has the same point count and ordering. Attribute Copy is faster and avoids interpolation artifacts because it assigns values directly by matching indices or IDs. A common misunderstanding is to use Attribute Copy when topologies differ; that leads to misaligned data or missing attributes. Before copying, always confirm identical point counts or a reliable ID mapping. If you need partial copying, use a custom ID attribute to limit which points receive values. When topology differs but shapes are similar, prefer Attribute Transfer instead. In short, pick Copy for exact index or ID matches and Transfer for shape-based projection. Attribute Copy SOP — Exact Matches means use attribute copy for index- or id-matched geometries to preserve exact values without interpolation; use transfer when topology differs.. In practical terms, copy attributes between geometries by index or id. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: When to copy
keyIdea.text: Use Attribute Copy for index- or ID-matched geometries to preserve exact values without interpolation; use Transfer when topology differs.

content.html:
Core Tool

Attribute Copy SOP

Copy attributes by matching point/primitive indices or by using a custom ID attribute. Ideal when source and destination are topologically identical or intentionally indexed.

Practical example
After a simulation on a proxy mesh, use Attribute Copy to transfer the velocity attribute back to the original high-res mesh that shares the same point order.
Key Takeaway

Copy when indices or IDs align; transfer when shapes align but topology differs.

Checklist before copying
  • Confirm identical point counts or a reliable custom ID attribute.
  • Verify attribute names and types match between source and destination.
  • Test on a subset of points to ensure mapping behaves as expected.
Common mistake
Assuming two similarly shaped meshes have matching indices. Always check ordering or provide explicit IDs.

screens.title: Cross-Component Access: prim() and point()
screens.subtitle: Read attributes from different component types with VEX

narration.text: VEX functions prim() and point() let you read attributes from components other than the one your wrangle is running over. For example, when iterating over points you can use prim(0, "Cd", @primnum) to read a primitive color that the point belongs to. Similarly, in a primitive wrangle you can call point(0, "P", i) to sample the position of a specific point index. These functions are essential when attributes across classes must influence each other, such as setting point attributes based on primitive material tags or computing a per-primitive mask from neighboring point weights. A concrete code example in the chapter computes average velocity as a detail attribute by iterating through points with point() and dividing by npoints(). That pattern is straightforward: sum values with point(), then divide by the count to store a single detail attribute. A misconception is trying to use prim() without the correct index context; ensure you pass the right component index such as @primnum or an explicit loop counter. When you need more control over aggregation or non-standard mapping, VEX provides the flexibility to compute exactly the statistic you require.

keyIdea.title: VEX access
keyIdea.text: Use prim() and point() to bridge attribute classes; they enable custom aggregation and mapping that SOP nodes cannot always express.

content.html:
VEX Techniques

prim() and point()

Read attributes from other component types to build relationships between points, primitives, and the whole geometry.

Example: compute average velocity (chapter example)
// Run Over: Detail
vector total_velocity = {0,0,0};
int num_points = npoints(0); // Get total number of points from input 0

for (int i = 0; i < num_points; i++) {
  total_velocity += point(0, "v", i); // Sum up all point velocities
}
v@avg_velocity = total_velocity / (float)num_points; // Calculate average and store as new detail attribute
Practical tips
  • When in a point wrangle, use prim(0, "attr", @primnum) to sample primitive attributes related to the point.
  • Pass explicit indices into point() or prim() when sampling arbitrary elements.
  • Use detail wrangles to store global aggregates computed from individual components.
Key Takeaway

prim() and point() provide controlled access across classes; use them for custom summaries and mappings that SOPs cannot express directly.

screens.title: Attribute Interpolation — Why it matters
screens.subtitle: How averaging and blend width shape the final result

narration.text: Attribute interpolation is the mathematical process that computes intermediate attribute values during transfers or promotions. When transferring attributes by proximity, Blend Width determines the falloff curve—how much influence a nearby source point has on a destination point relative to distance. For promotion from point to primitive, choosing Average is itself an interpolation: the primitive's value is the mean of its corner points. These interpolation choices directly affect visual continuity, animation behavior, and numerical properties like weight normalization. For example, averaging vertex colors often softens color transitions but can also mute high-frequency detail that matters for wear or masks. A common mistake is relying on a single parameter for all cases; thin features, sharp seams, and masks require different interpolation strategies. In game contexts interpolation affects vertex lighting and blending between LODs, so test in the final target environment. If you need control beyond built-in methods, compute your interpolation explicitly in VEX where you can choose weighting functions, clamp values, or normalize results to maintain sums or ranges. Reflect on whether you want smoothness or fidelity, then pick the method that preserves the property you care about most.

keyIdea.title: Interpolation principle
keyIdea.text: Interpolation choices determine whether transfers prioritize smooth transitions or preserve local detail; pick methods and parameters based on the property you need to preserve.

content.html:
Concept

Attribute Interpolation

Interpolation calculates intermediate values during transfer or promotion. Choices like Blend Width and Average determine smoothness versus fidelity.

Smoothness
Large blend widths and averaging create smooth transitions but may blur details.
Fidelity
Small blend widths and per-element mapping preserve local detail but risk patchiness.
Practical guidance
  • Decide whether you need smoothness or exactness for the attribute in question.
  • For weights and lighting data, prefer smooth interpolation and validate in the renderer or game engine.
  • For masks or crisp decals, use tighter thresholds or copy by index when possible.
Key Takeaway

Interpolation changes semantics: choose methods that preserve the attribute property—sum, mean, or local detail—you need for downstream use.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Sphere Cd → Box + Promote to Detail
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step from ramp to transferred and promoted Cd

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough follows the chapter's lab: create a source sphere with a Cd ramp, transfer to a box, then promote Cd to detail. Start by adding a Sphere configured to Polygons with moderate frequency. Create an Attribute Wrangle running over points using a ramp parameter to assign Cd along the Y axis. Use that wrangle's color ramp to sculpt a colorful vertical gradient. For the destination, add a Box sized to match the sphere roughly. Insert an Attribute Transfer node with the sphere as first input and the box as second input. In the transfer node list Cd under Attributes to Transfer, then tune Distance Threshold until most box points sample the sphere. Use Blend Width to soften or sharpen edges. Append a Color SOP set to From Attributes to visualize the result. Finally, add an Attribute Promote node to convert Cd from Point to Detail, selecting Average as the Promotion Method. Open the Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect Cd on the Point tab after transfer and on the Detail tab after promote. This sequence teaches practical parameter tuning and verification techniques you will reuse in production.

keyIdea.title: Lab focus
keyIdea.text: Follow the transfer then promote sequence and validate results in the geometry spreadsheet; practice tuning thresholds and blend for a clean transfer.

content.html:
Hands-on Lab

Walkthrough Steps

1. Create source
Sphere → Polygon, Frequency 10. Add an Attribute Wrangle (Points) with a color ramp parameter to assign Cd along Y.
2. Create destination
Box sized ~2,2,2 with low divisions to receive the transferred Cd.
3. Transfer attributes
Attribute Transfer: connect sphere to input 1 and box to input 2. Add Cd to Attributes to Transfer, tune Distance Threshold and Blend Width.
4. Visualize and promote
Add Color From Attributes to view Cd. Then Attribute Promote: Original Name Cd, Original Class Point, New Class Detail, Method Average.
Checkpoints
  • After transfer: confirm Cd exists on points in the geometry spreadsheet.
  • After promote: confirm Cd appears on the Detail tab as a single aggregated value.
  • If transfer looks patchy: slightly increase Distance Threshold or add source density.
Key Takeaway

This lab combines projection and promotion: practice parameter tuning and always verify attributes in the spreadsheet.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Diagnose patchiness, bleeding, and index mismatches

narration.text: Troubleshooting attribute workflows saves time. If transfer results are patchy, first check Distance Threshold—too small and destination points can fail to find sources. Increase the threshold incrementally or increase source density. If you observe unwanted bleeding of attributes into unrelated areas, lower the threshold and shrink Blend Width. For Attribute Promote, verify that you chose the correct promotion method: Average changes magnitudes, Sum accumulates, and Min/Max pick extrema; select the one that preserves the semantics you need. When Attribute Copy yields wrong values, confirm identical point counts or that a reliable ID attribute is used. A silent failure often means indices differ; examine point counts and ordering in the geometry spreadsheet. Use the Color SOP to visualize attributes at each stage and open the Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect raw numbers. A useful habit is to perform incremental checks after each node: transfer, visualize, then promote, rather than applying multiple operations at once. This isolates where a bad value originates. Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting means patchy transfers: increase threshold or source density. bleeding: reduce threshold or blend. copy errors: verify point counts or id mapping.. In practical terms, diagnose patchiness, bleeding, and index mismatches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Patchy transfers: increase threshold or source density. Bleeding: reduce threshold or blend. Copy errors: verify point counts or ID mapping.

content.html:
Debugging

Common Mistakes

  • Distance Threshold too low → patchy or missing transfers.
  • Distance Threshold too high → bleeding and loss of locality.
  • Using Copy when indices differ → misaligned or wrong attribute values.
  • Assuming Average preserves totals when it reduces magnitude.
Quick fixes
  1. Visualize attributes after each node with Color From Attributes.
  2. Open Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect raw values and counts.
  3. Test on a small subset so changes are fast to iterate.
Warning

Never copy attributes between meshes unless you have verified index or ID correspondence; silent mismatches are common and destructive.

screens.title: When to Use Transfer, Promote, or Copy
screens.subtitle: Decision rules for clean attribute workflows

narration.text: Choosing the right tool avoids wasted work. Use Attribute Transfer when source and destination differ topologically but are similar in shape—this projects attributes by proximity and interpolates results for mismatched meshes. Use Attribute Copy when you have the same topology or a reliable ID mapping; Copy is precise and fast. Use Attribute Promote to change attribute class or to produce coarser or global summaries, selecting Average, Sum, Min, or Max according to the numeric property you must preserve. If you need a custom aggregation or normalization not covered by Promote's methods, write a brief VEX wrangle using point() or prim() to compute exactly the statistic you need. In production pipelines, combine these tools: project fine detail with Transfer, then Promote to a detail value for metadata, or Copy simulation output back to the high-res mesh when indices align. The mental model to keep is: Transfer = shape-based projection, Copy = index-based exactness, Promote = class conversion and aggregation. Use the geometry spreadsheet at every decision point to validate the outcome.
